20/02/2023). Early opinion polls have pointed to a tight contested
election in May, with some early polls showing opposition coalition
parties leading (Al Jazeera 30/01/2023; France 24 22/01/2023;
OSW 24/01/2023; PolitPro 31/01/2023). The anti-refugee public
sentiment in Türkiye has been increasing in the past years accord-
ing to opinion polls, in combination with the decline of the economic
situation generating competition over jobs and services (Arab News
06/02/2022; NPA Syria 19/01/2023; Al Jazeera 30/01/2023; The
New Arab 24/06/2022; SWP 21/02/2020; Al Jazeera 27/07/2022).
The Turkish Government had already announced in 2022 the
construction of more than 68,000 prefabricated briquette houses
in areas of Northwest Syria for the return of Syrian refugees (VOA
26/09/2022; Global Voices 08/05/2022). The construction of
these houses is part of the bigger project to establish residential
compounds in 13 areas of northern Syria, which would eventually
absorb one million Syrian refugees from Türkiye (Al-Monitor
08/05/2022; Sabah 05/05/2022). Around a half million Syrians have
already voluntary returned to Syria, some because of economic
hardship, discrimination, and a general feeling of being unsafe in
Türkiye (MEMO 03/10/2022; SCF 27/9/2022).
The earthquakes that hit southeastern Türkiye and northwestern
Syria in February 2023 could increase the resentment towards
refugees, as competition over public services and housing would
likely increase. The deterioration of humanitarian conditions in
Northwest Syria as a result of the earthquakes will pose challenges
and delay the Turkish Government’s plans to return Syrian refugees
to the region.
trigger:
- Escalation in the anti-migrant sentiment and rhetoric

- New emerging geopolitical situation regarding with Russia, US, Government of Syria, and opposition factions

- Kurdish conflict escalation, especially near the boarders with Syria
vulnerability:
The influx of returnees will put a strain on
infrastructure and limited resources, worsening humanitarian
needs in the area

 The February earthquakes highly
affected northwestern Syria, killing more than 51,000 people,
injuring more than 120,000, and damaging more than 220,000
buildings, including hospitals

Prior to the earthquake, Northwest Syria was
already hosting 2.9 million IDPs, with 1.8 million living in camps.
Four million people relied on humanitarian assistance, with 3.3
million being food insecure

Northwest Syria faces very high humanitarian access constrains in
an area where politics and humanitarian issues overlap. Cross-bor-
der and crossline operations have been highly constrained and
since 2014 regularly re-negotiated at the UNSC level. Aid for
Northwest Syria is highly politicised and has been limited by
authorities in charge of different areas. Damaged infrastructure
from the conflict and earthquakes further complicates humani-
tarian access in the region, potentially hampering the provision
of assistance to returnees

Many returnees to Syria are facing grave human rights violations,
torture, and blackmail by the Government of Syria and the different
opposition militias. Future returnees from Türkiye are likely to face
similar protection concerns

On the longer term, if the areas of return would
come under the control of the Syrian army – whether to prevent
Turkish advancement or in coordination with Türkiye – there
would be heightened concerns for the safety of those perceived
by the Government of Syria as opposition figures and activists

risk_title: Heightened military response following increased territorial control of and collaboration among anti-military resistance forces results in intensified conflict across most of the country, leading to a deterioration of the humanitarian situation
rationale:
Myanmar’s military is currently facing a conflict of scale and intensity they had never faced before. It is estimated that the junta and its militias have full control only of nearly 30% of the 330 townships of Myanmar. Around 60% of the townships are either contested or under the control of anti-military resistance groups.

The February 2021 coup by the Myanmar military was followed by the formation of a government in exile called the National Unity Government (NUG) and its armed wing, the People’s Defense Forces (PDFs), with the NUG acting as a parallel government in the areas under its control. Since the coup, the PDFs have been in intense conflict with the military. Through time, the PDFs have been enhancing their capacities, including by adopting innovative technologies (such as weaponised drones). Since 2022, there has been increased collaboration between the PDFs and ethnic armed organisations on military training, the supply of arms, and common defensive and offensive strategies. On the other hand, the junta’s military has been losing personnel because of injuries, defections, and desertions, leading it to tap into other forces, such as the police and militias, for support. It has also issued a ‘right to arms’ policy allowing civilians to access weapons, with the aim of facilitating the creation of new or the expansion of existing pro-military junta militias.

Because of the increased territorial control of and collaboration among anti-military resistance forces, the military and its affiliated militias are expected to increase operations in the coming months to gain back lost territories and reduce the strength of resistance forces. As a result, conflict will escalate across most of the country. The military is likely to increase air strikes, especially as a result of congenial non-monsoon weather conditions, to conduct air operations. It is also likely to attack civilians and infrastructure, heightening constraints on humanitarian access. The junta has already employed this tactic to force anti-military resistance groups to use up their resources for meeting the needs of conflict-affected populations and to cut off such groups from their access to food, finances, intelligence, and recruits. 

Impact:
- An escalation of fighting across the vast majority of the country will likely increase the number of IDPs to 2.4 million in the third quarter of 2023, as per OCHA 2023 projections. 

- Many people will likely flee conflict-affected areas to remote locations, such as jungles, which are cut off from any services and beyond the reach of humanitarian responders. 

- Displacement will increase protection threats, such as family separation, psychological distress, gender-based violence, and human trafficking. 

- Intensification of conflict will likely result in agriculture inputs and infrastructure to be damaged and looted, and landmines and explosive remnants of war will contaminate croplands. Many farmers will be forced to leave their lands, losing their source of livelihood. The food production gap will further increase, heightening food insecurity and malnutrition. Increased movement restrictions, the rapid depreciation of currency and inflation, high fertiliser and fuel costs, and a lack of government support for farmers will also heighten the loss of livelihood and food insecurity situation.

Update:
This risk has materialised. Armed conflict has intensified in most parts of the country, especially in the months of June, July, and August 2023. The military junta extended the state of emergency in July 2023 for an additional six months and ramped up efforts to gain lost territories in many parts of the country. 

Conflict has continued to damage and destroy vital civilian infrastructure, such as healthcare facilities and schools, and resulted in civilian casualties. 

As at 28 August, the number of post-coup IDPs was around 1.65 million, taking the total IDPs in the country to around 1.96 million. A lot of the displaced live in makeshift shelters or in remote places, such as forests and jungles, which are cut off from any services and difficult to reach by humanitarian responders. 

Reduced agricultural production in 2022 resulted in income losses and increased food prices. The devastating impact of Cyclone Mocha also worsened the food insecurity and malnutrition situations in the country.
trigger:
- Increased territorial control of and collaboration among anti-military resistance forces

- Enhanced capacities of anti-military forces, including by adopting innovative technologies (such as weaponised drones)

- Growing political instability with no sign of cooperation to de-escalate the conflict between the military junta and anti-military forces
vulnerability:
- People fleeing the conflict-affected areas to remote locations, such as jungles, are cut off from any services and beyond the reach of humanitarian responders. 

- Displaced people will be exposed to increased protection risks, such as family separation, psychological distress, gender-based violence, and human trafficking. Women and girls are especially vulnerable to protection risks.

- Intensified conflict will further increase food production gap , heightening food insecurity and malnutrition. 

- Farmers are likely to lose their livelihoods due to the growing conflict

risk_title: Increased food needs following the conflict between SAF and RSF
rationale:
As at 11 May, conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) had resulted in over 600 fatalities and 5,500 injuries. Over 700,000 have become internally displaced.
Levels of food insecurity will likely deteriorate, affecting between two and 2.5 million more people. Food needs will likely increase, and the biggest spikes in food insecurity will likely be in West Darfur, West Kordofan, Blue Nile, Red Sea, and North Darfur states. 
The price of basic food items will likely increase by 25% in the next three to six months because of disruptions to the agricultural season (June - August) and to supply chains due to fighting and insecurity. People's access to food aid will likely be restricted because of challenges facing humanitarians to operate in conflict-affected areas and looting of their assets. 
If the rainy season (June - October) caused severe floods similar to the rainy season in 2022, it will likely affect crops, reducing the availability of food. Humanitarian access will likely be further restricted.
trigger:
- Continuation of armed clashes between SAF and RSF.
- Restricted humanitarian access.
- Disruption to supply chains. 
- Disruption to the planting and harvest seasons. 
- Severe flood season in 2023.
vulnerability: People are already highly vulnerable because of pre-existing humanitarian issues in Sudan, including intercommunal clashes and socio-economic challenges. Lack of security and restrict ired humanitarian access to the people in need will increase their vulnerability.

risk_title: Increasing insecurity and tensions in eastern Chad following an influx of refugees from Darfur
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Some 100,000 Sudanese have crossed into Chad between 15 April and 1 June, and it is likely that another 200,000 people will cross in the following three months. The majority of them are from West Darfur state, where intercommunal clashes escalated following the clashes between the SAF and RSF. It is likely that the influx of Sudanese refugees into eastern border areas of Chad will destabilise security because it increases competition over limited sources such as water. This will likely also trigger tribal tensions between the host community and refugees, as the region has witnessed tensions between Arabs and non-Arabs for decades. Insecurity in Chad will likely increase because Darfur, which shares long borders with Chad, is likely to become the epicentre of foreign fighters, with an increase in arming and presence of weapons. In case of increased insecurity and clashes in eastern Sudan, many people will likely be displaced, including from refugee camps. Humanitarian access will likely be affected too, restricting the delivery of aid to people in need. 

As at December 2023, there are some reports indicating that tensions has increased following the influx of refugees from Sudan, but no clashes are reported. This is mainly because of lack of food resources, driven by increased demand and reduced harvest. Chad experienced one of the worst lean seasons that negatively affected the harvest. More members of the host community are demanding food for themselves at distribution centres. Others are moving internally to other areas because of lack of resources, where the majority of refugee are being hosted.
trigger:
- influx of more refugees from Darfur to Chad
- increase in competition over sources
- increase tribal tensions
- increased arming in Darfur
vulnerability: Both the Sudanese refugees and the host community are already highly vulnerable and have limited sources. The camps are overcrowded, and water sources are limited. Humanitarian response is challenging because of funding shortfalls.

risk_title: The upcoming Russian presidential elections increase administrative coercion and violence in occupied areas of Ukraine, heightening access constraints to critical services and protection concerns
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Rationale
The Russian presidential elections are due in March 2024 and the current president Vladimir Putin is likely to run for a fifth term. Putin is likely to use the elections to legitimise the Russian presence in Ukraine internationally, through pro Russia media and organisations, and by seeking recognition statements from ally countries, like Syria and DPRK.  
Russian authorities and Russian forces have previously coerced and intimidated people in the occupied areas to vote in the yearly Russian regional elections held in September 2023. The same happened during the the Russian-staged referend to annex Luhansk, and parts of Donetsk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts on 30 September 2022, similarly to Crimea in 2014.
Russian authorities are likely to increase threats and violence to pressure participation in the elections heightening the risks to personal safety and protection for people residing in the occupied areas, notably through detention of civilians.
A Russian decree of April 2023 stipulates that people without a Russian passport in the occupied areas are retroactively considered ‘’foreigners’’ or ‘’stateless’’ as of 30 September 2022, and must apply for a residence permit or risk forcible displacement by July 2024. Forcible displacement, however, has been ongoing since the 2022 full-scale invasion.
The Russian campaign to fast-track citizenship started in 2014 in Crimea. In 2019, it spread to Russian controlled parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, and it has been accelerating since 2022. The imposition of Russian passports or coercing civilians into voting through threats and violence will likely increase significantly in the lead up to the Russian presidential elections.  Widespread and systematic violence is already used against civilians to consolidate control. 

Impact 
At least 5 million people are estimated to live in areas occupied by Russia, with some 1.5 million Russian passports issued since 2022.  Those who refuse Russian passports are increasingly vulnerable to violence, forced displacement, detention, filtration on the Russian borders, and loss of documentation and property. Detained civilians are at a high risk of torture, sexual abuse, and ill-treatment, with at least 25,000 people considered missing in detention as at September 2023.
Men will be at heightened risk of forced conscription by the Russian military, and might cope by hiding, putting further financial burden on families, particularly women, while more children will be sent to military youth camps.
Since 2022, at least 19,500 children were illegally transferred from Ukraine into Russia by Russian authorities. Unaccompanied children become at risk of inadequate living conditions, family separation, psychological trauma, physical abuse including SGBV, hunger, and potentially forced conscription after turning 18.
People who do not accept Russian passports will further have reduced access to essential services and livelihoods, such as healthcare, education, employment, and social protection. Protracted lack of access to healthcare, medicines, and specialised care, puts the older people at higher risk of death that is otherwise preventable. 
Social cohesion will decrease due to tensions between those who accept Russian passports and those who do not, in addition to crime, looting and violence resulting from the increased presence of Russian armed forces.

Updates: 

As at end of November 2023, Russia is reportedly planning an intensification campaign in the occupied territories aiming to increase the number of local population with Russian passports to 85%. This intensification is likely linked to the Russian presidential elections in 2024.

Russian authorities continue to use basic service access to pressure the population into getting Russian passports, through restricting access to Russian passport holders only; withholding high school diplomas, preventing new school year registration, threats of forcible displacement into Russia, threats to take away children from parents, private property confiscation, and access denial to healthcare and essential medication.

In February 2024, an 80-year-old woman who relies on a wheel chair was rescued from an occupied village in Donetsk oblast because she was unwilling to take Russian citizenship and the Russian authorities refused to pay her pension.

The election took place on 15-17 March in Russia, however the Russian authorities conducted early so-called voting in the occupied areas in Ukraine in February 2024. Despite not holding Russian passports, some Ukrainian citizens were still expected to participate in the so-called elections, likely in an attempt to increase the number of so-called votes. In some areas, Russian authorities, were accompanied by military personnel, and went door to door with voting boxes and ballots.

This risk has materialised, and the pressure to accept Russian passports continues through restrictions on movement and various services, including any administrative services such as car registration, medical care and education as well as fear of being conscripted into the Russian army is forcing people to leave their homes though the only crossing between Russian and Ukraine in Sumska oblast; a km unpaved road which people have to cross on foot, however it is more affordable than traveling through the EU. In late April 2024, an 88 year old man was forced to leave his home in the occupied areas, and walk by foot to Ukraine controlled territory after the Russian authorities confiscated his Ukrainian ID in order to force him into accepting the Russian citizenship which he refused.  

There are cases of farmers being interrogated with the use of physical violence about not obtaining a Russian passport and re-registering their business. 

As of 1 July, people who have not accepted a Russian passport can be forcefully deported if they do not register as a so-called ''stateless person or a foreigner'' and undergo a medical examination, and mandatory fingerprinting and photographic documentation by the Russian authorities and they cannot stay in the occupied territories more than 90 days out of every 180 days of the year. If a person wants to work, they must obtain a paid approval from the Russian authorities.
trigger: - Additional constraints put by Russian authorities on the local population without a Russian passport when accessing specific services in the occupied areas (during the period of the March 2024 Russian presidential election season)
vulnerability: Any civilians who refuse Russian passports. Men with Russian passports are at risk of forced conscription.

risk_title: El Niño in Zimbabwe increases the needs of those already affected by drought, cyclones, disease outbreaks, and protracted economic instability
rationale:
The World Meteorological Organization has announced the beginning of El Niño, which has a 90% probability of continuing through the second half of 2023. During the November 2023 to March 2024 period, El Niño is expected to drive drier conditions than average in Zimbabwe. This period coincides with the agricultural season, which might significantly affect crop planting, growth, and harvest.

In 2023, an estimated three million people, including two million children, will need humanitarian assistance as a result of the effects of drought, Cyclone Freddy, floods, disease outbreaks, and the protracted economic crisis in the country. Priority needs include nutrition, health, protection, education, and WASH services.

The effects of El Niño could heighten the needs of the people in Zimbabwe who have not fully recovered from the impact of currently below-average rainfall, cyclones, disease outbreaks, and economic instability. The reduction in yield and scarcity of water resulting from El Niño would respectively lead to increased food insecurity and heighten WASH needs. Water scarcity is likely to lead to the spread of endemic diseases, such as cholera and typhoid, which can result from poor sanitation and water contamination.
trigger:
- Already existing below-average rainfall
- Economic instability and the Government's inability to respond fast
- The upcoming elections as an aggravating factor
vulnerability: In 2023, UNICEF estimates that three million people, including two million children, will need humanitarian assistance in Zimbabwe. A further worsening of the situation might lead those affected to adopt negative coping mechanisms, such as reducing the number of meals, early marriages, and transactional sex.

risk_title: Increased Russian attacks on grain infrastructure and ports in Ukraine after withdrawal from the Grain Deal results in more casualties and economic deterioration
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Russia’s withdrawal from the Black Sea Grain Initiative, also known as the Grain Deal, was followed by an intensification of attacks targeting Ukraine’s grain storage infrastructure, ports and southern cities. The withdrawal in July 2023 came at the beginning of the harvest season in Ukraine. In a period of one month since withdrawal, at least 270,000 tonnes of grain were damaged by the attacks. Russia carried out 14 attacks –between 11 July and 23 August– hitting grain terminals, warehouses, port infrastructure, industrial equipment, and administrative buildings, as well as grain storage facilities in ports on the Black Sea and Danube River. Zatoka bridge, a key transport route for grain to Izmail, was also hit.
Targeted attacks on grain export routes will result in more casualties and potential displacement. Agriculture is already heavily impacted by the conflict. A drop in grain export will lead to increased stockpiling of grain and could force farmers to reduce sowing in the next harvesting season. Increasing cost of transportation and storage of grain, compounded with increasing insecurity at grain facilities will impact the safety and socioeconomics of Ukrainian farmers, households, and businesses that depend on agricultural livelihoods and exports.

Updates:

By October 2023, Russia destroyed 300,000 metric tonnes of grain in its attacks on Ukraine. 

On 9 November 2023, a Russian missile strike damaged a civilian ship under the flag of Liberia as it was entering Odesa port. Between August and November, Odesa port was attacked 21 times by the Russian military. 

Despite the end of the grain deal, Ukraine managed to export 4.3 million metric tons of grain in October 2023. 

In November 2023, an investigation concluded that Russia planned a systemic takeover of agricultural resources, including seizing grain, agricultural machinery and facilities from farmers and agricultural businesses in Ukraine prior to the full-scale invasion in 2022. Since then, Russia made 1 billion from selling the grain it seized, and findings show that Russia has used the illegally made profit to fund the war.

The estimated agricultural losses doubled from USD 40 billion in May 2023, to USD 80 billion by February 2024.
trigger:
- The harvest season start in July
- Russia pulled out of the grain deal in July
- Russian long-term plans to block Ukraine's access to the Black Sea as part of the full-scale invasion
vulnerability: Farmers, families and businesses relying on agricultural livelihoods are particularly the most vulnerable.

risk_title: ATMIS withdrawal from Somalia leads to the expansion and increased activity of Al-Shabaab, increasing needs in recaptured and conflict-affected areas
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
There is increased risk of the ATMIS withdrawal leading to a security vacuum in Somalia. With an arms embargo is still in place, the ATMIS has been providing military equipment and other logistical support to the Somali Security Forces (SSF), besides being key to holding and guaranteeing security in recaptured areas previously taken by Al-Shabaab (such as areas in Banadir, Galgaduud, Hiran, Lower Shabelle, and even Middle Shabelle). The SSF do not receive funding and international backing, and the ATMIS withdrawal may signal a downward trend in the country's security and compromise the military capabilities of the SSF against Al-Shabaab, especially since increased Al-Shabaab attacks have coincided with the ATMIS drawdown of troops since January 2023.

The increase in areas liberated from Al-Shabaab does not automatically mean improved security or increased humanitarian presence. Previously recaptured areas by the SSF remain inaccessible to humanitarians because of the use of explosive devices along main supply routes by Al-Shabaab.

Increased Al-Shabaab attacks will deteriorate the humanitarian situation of communities in recaptured areas and areas with planned counterinsurgency operations in the south. Besides the ATMIS withdrawal, the current political infighting in the south that has stalled the start of the second face of the counterinsurgency would also give Al-Shabaab room to plan and regroup. The continued support to the SSF of clan militias also remains uncertain because of political infighting in some states.
trigger:
- Al Shabaab intensifies attacks including the use of rockets with the start of the second round of the Government's counter-insurgency operations in southern Somalia in August 2023, causing high impact damage to infrastructure as well as risking civilian lives
- The 90-day postponement of the withdrawal of 3,000 ATMIS troops (that was to take place end of September 2023) contributes in holding recaptured territory from Al-Shabaab, particularly in Galmudug and Hirshabelle
-Al Shabaab intensifies attacks against local officials to discourage/ weaken support for the Government's counter-insurgency campaign in central and southern Somalia. This limits movement by local officials to administer newly liberated areas increasing Al-Shabaab's chances or regaining these territories
-Al Shabaab renegotiates with clan elders to recover lost territories and regain local support, which affects military operations against them
-Increased clan competition in Jubaland, southern Somalia, creates a power imbalance thus reducing clan support for the counter-insurgency campaign
vulnerability: Population estimates for areas where the counterinsurgency operations have been conducted is over five million. These areas include Banadir, Galgaduud, Hiran, Lower Shabelle, Middle Shabelle, and Mudug. Affected populations will likely flee to rural/inaccessible areas away from humanitarian assistance, increasing their reliance on negative coping mechanisms for basic needs, including food. Drought is also continuing in conflict-affected areas.

risk_title: Increased fighting and power and gas supply disruptions severely limit people’s ability to access heating, resulting in loss of life and increased acute humanitarian needs in Russian-controlled areas and areas of active ground conflict in the southeast
risk_type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
rationale:
This risk was raised in ACAPS October 2022 Global Risk report and materialised during the 2022-2023 winter season. It will likely materialise again during the 2023-2024 winter season. Attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine are ongoing, however, with the start of the cold season in October, the Russian armed forces will likely ramp up attacks against heating and electric energy production infrastructure to disrupt the provision of power. The Government of Ukraine has been preparing the energy sector for the winter, conducting repairs, strengthening air defence of key infrastructure, and accumulating gas and coal reserves. The high-voltage power grid will only be repaired to an estimated 30-40% of its pre-full-scale invasion capacity. Officials have warned that 2023-24 winter will be more difficult than the last, as the country has a significantly impacted energy sector, that will have limited margins to cope with additional shocks.
These challenges will happen while many households in Ukraine struggle with limited income opportunities due to job loss and/or displacement, meaning that many may not have the means to purchase winter items such as generators, batteries, heating fuel, clothes, blankets, or to repair damaged houses ahead of winter. The impact will be especially high in frontline and occupied areas where humanitarian needs are significant and humanitarian access highly constrained. By August 2023, only 4% of the people who received aid live in occupied areas.  Older people are particularly vulnerable to harsh winter conditions. The lack of food, medicines and adequate housing can result in preventable deaths.

Update:
Air defenses are concentrated in the capital city of Kyiv, while the rest of the country is not fully protected from attacks, and the energy infrastructure remains vulnerable in the winter of 2023/2024.

Russia has resumed attacks on energy infrastructure in the winter season of 2023/2024 as predicted. In late November, as temperatures started to reach below zero, Russia launched the largest drone attack since 2022 with 75 drones on 25 November. 

One of the main thermal power plants in a frontline oblast was attacked for the fifth time within one month on the night of 27 November. 

Russia launched the largest attack since 2022 on 29 November 2023 with 158 ballistic missiles. 

In February 2024, Russia received 400 ballistic missiles from Iran. 

On 22 March, Russia launched one of the largest mass (combined drone and missile) attacks against Ukraine, targeting Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Kryvyi Rih cities, primarily aiming at the energy infrastructure.  The large-scale attack targeted Khmelnytskyi, Odesa, Mykolaiv, Vinnytsia, Kirovohrad, Sumy, Lviv, Poltava, and Ivano-Frankivsk oblasts as well. Ukraine's largest hydroelectric power plant, the Dnipro Hydroelectric Station in the southern Zaporizhzhia oblast was damaged in the attack. There was almost a complete power loss in Kharkiv city where energy infrastructure was hit as well. Critical infrastructure in Dnipropetrovsk oblast was also hit. Ukraine's largest private energy company lost 50% of its generating capacity in the 22 March attack, and it will months to recover from the damage. The attack left more than one million people without power. The intensification of attacks on energy infrastructure continued across the country in late March. During March 2024 alone, the Russian forces reportedly launched over 400 missiles, 600 drones, and 3,000 guided aerial bombs.

In Odesa, two districts introduced partial blackout on 31 March, however that same day, power was restored. As at 1 April, all the energy infrastructure in Kharkiv city is destroyed and blackouts were reintroduced. An additional 109 generators, 19 heat and power cogeneration units, and 13 emergency vehicles were provided in April in response to the intensified attacks on energy infrastructure. 

On 11 April, a major power plant near Kyiv was completely destroyed by Russian air strikes. The impact will affect energy supply next winter, according to the assessment by authorities. Two other thermal power plants were significantly damaged in the west of Ukraine, adding strain on electricity supply in the country, and overall resulting in Ukraine needing to import energy.

By May 2024, 70% of Ukraine's energy production capability was down because of the systemic Russian attacks.
trigger: - Start of the cold season in October amidst ongoing Russian full scale war against Ukraine.
vulnerability: Elderly people, people with chronic diseases and disabilities

risk_title: Increased political and ethnic tensions and armed conflict expansion in Sudan lead to mass displacements and unmet needs
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The conflict between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) that escalated on 15 April 2023 had already killed 13,900 people as at 23 February and internally displaced 6.3 million as at 23 February. The conflict has particularly affected Darfur region, which has experienced the largest numbers of fatalities and displacements. Since mid-April, there have been increasing reports of killings and ethnically motivated attacks by the RSF and their allies from Arab militias, especially against the Masalit community. RSF fighters are targeting injured non-Arab civilians as they are receiving treatment at hospitals and displaced people at checkpoints. As a result, calls are increasing among civilians in the region to arm and defend themselves, potentially escalating armed conflict. Khartoum city and Kordofan region also saw an intensification of fighting in September, with the SAF committing acts of sexual assault and targeted attacks. Armed conflict will likely increase over key strategic positions and specific areas, such as Port Sudan city, where there are seaports, the only operating airport, and humanitarian hubs. Competition over limited sources of food and water between Arabs and non-Arabs can contribute to increasing tensions, especially with West Darfur state having the highest food insecurity levels across Sudan. Between July–September 2023, about 62% of the Sudanese population were projected to be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity levels or worse.

Impact   
The total population of Sudan will likely be exposed to the geographic expansion of clashes, resulting in more displacements, increased needs for shelter, water, food, and medical care, and the further restriction of humanitarian access. The impacts will likely affect the ten million people living in Darfur region the most. Between 15 April and 16 August, nearly 1.2 million people were already displaced from Darfur. With more clashes, the numbers will likely be higher. Most displacement will likely remain internal, except from West Darfur where people will continue to go to Chad. Needs for shelter, water, food, and medical care will increase. The IDP/refugee camps in Chad had already reached their capacity before the influx from West Darfur, and there will likely be a need to establish more camps. Humanitarian organisations are already facing challenges to deliver aid in Darfur region. Between 3–5 August, WFP delivered their first food assistance convoy since 15 April to West Darfur. With very limited aid delivery and high insecurity, people’s needs will likely remain unmet, especially health needs given the targeting of hospitals.
trigger:
- Longstanding tensions in Darfur
- Targeted attacks on the Masalit and non-Arab tribes
- Civilians obtaining more weapons
- Limited resources and increased food insecurity
- Targeting of key strategic points across Sudan
vulnerability: The conflict has displaced millions internally and outside Sudan. Humanitarian needs are high, and humanitarian access is restricted. Despite the response and presence of humanitarian organisations, the affected people are considered highly vulnerable.

risk_title: An escalation of clashes between Hezbollah and Israel, coinciding with conflict escalation between Palestine and Israel, results in displacement, infrastructure damage, and humanitarian needs in southern Lebanon
rationale:
RATIONALE: The Blue Line, a disputed border area between Lebanon and Israel, has always been a source of tension between the two countries, who have been at war twice already, the latest being in 2006. Hezbollah — a political party and militant group mostly representative of the Shia population in southern Lebanon, with the backing Iran — has been the main entity fighting against Israel in Lebanon in the past. Since the beginning of 2023, there has been a growing number of breaches of international commitments on the Blue Line, which has been patrolled by UNIFIL. There has also been an increase in provocative actions near the border area from both sides, besides increased confrontations and escalation of rhetoric. Hezbollah has been setting up tents near the border, and Israeli fighter jets have been flying over the area. Both sides have conducted military drills and made many attempts to cross the border. Hezbollah and Israel are unlikely to enter into a full-scale war in Lebanon. However, any provocative action from the two sides amid increased tensions in the Blue Line area, or the increased involvement of Hezbollah and Iran in the Palestine-Israel conflict, which would trigger Israel’s reaction, could result in clashes or international armed conflict at the Lebanon-Israel border. As at 15 October, cross border attacks between Hezbollah and Lebanon are ongoing. Regional tensions in the Middle East, mainly between Israel and Iran, play a role in increasing clashes between Israel and Hezbollah. Israeli air strikes on Syria continue to target armed groups or cells backed by Iran (including some Hezbollah members) almost weekly, leading to more tensions with Hezbollah in Lebanon. The involvement of Palestinian armed groups based in refugee settlements in Lebanon (usually supported by Hezbollah) who sporadically clash with Israeli soldiers and attempt to cross the borders can also contribute to an escalation of fighting between Hezbollah and Israel. Together with the Palestinian Islamic Jihad, Hamas is one of the groups present in Lebanon and has fired rockets from Lebanon to Israel in the past.

IMPACT: The escalation of clashes at the Blue Line and air strikes by the Israeli Air Forces will likely expose up to 800,000 people in Lebanon to displacement and increased humanitarian needs. Already 29,000 people have been displaced between 14 – 26 October 2023, mostly to Tyre city, and they are staying with other families and at schools. A 33-day war between Lebanon and Israel in 2006 displaced an estimated 800,000 to 1 million people, mostly from northern Lebanon to mountain areas inside the country, as well as to neighbouring countries such as Syria. Fighting and air strikes are also likely to result in severe damage to critical infrastructure in targeted areas, such as Al Dahiya neighbourhood of Beirut city, which is predominantly inhabited by Shia Muslims. Many displaced people will stay in schools, mosques, and other public buildings, and shelter needs will be high. Priority needs will include food, medicine, safe drinking water, and NFIs. In 2023, an estimated 80% of Lebanon’s population live below the poverty line. Conflict will result in livelihood losses and further increase poverty.
trigger:
- a miscalculation of any provocative action from Hezbollah or Israel
- Ongoing airstrikes and Israeli ground operation in the Gaza Strip
- Increased tensions over the Blue Line
- Increase in breaches of international commitments on the Blue Line
- Increased regional tensions between Iran and Israel
vulnerability: People in Lebanon already face the impact of a deteriorating economy, high inflation, and loss of livelihoods. They are generally resilient to human-driven and climate crises, but an increase in clashes and displacement can increase their current needs and vulnerabilities caused or exacerbated by the socio-economic crisis.

risk_title: Water contamination and floods from Storm Daniel in Derna district are increasing the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks
rationale:
Between 9–11 September 2023, Storm Daniel caused flooding and destruction in the coastal areas of northeastern Libya, including the collapse of two dams in Derna district that killed thousands of people. As at 16 September, WHO had recorded almost 4,000 deaths, and more than 9,000 people were still missing. OCHA estimates that the floods affected 884,000 people to varying degrees. As at the end of September, more than 40,000 people were displaced, including at least 16,000 in Derna city and surrounding areas. People living in flood-affected areas are in urgent need of fresh water, as the floodwaters have washed away, buried in mud, or damaged entire residential zones, including water and sewage networks. Satellite imagery analysis indicates that over 2,200 buildings have been destroyed in the city. Half of the 18 boreholes for drinking water are also out of service. The consequent contamination of soil and groundwater, poor hygiene, and a lack of sanitation facilities are creating a risk of waterborne disease outbreaks, such as acute watery diarrhoea and cholera, and vector-borne disease outbreaks, such as malaria and typhoid, dengue, and yellow fever. Because of their more fragile immune systems, older people, children, and pregnant women are particularly at risk of these diseases. More than half of the 78 health facilities assessed by WHO in two districts and in Derna city are either closed or not functioning because of infrastructure damage and shortages of staff, medicine, supplies, and equipment. Given the weaknesses of the health system and the magnitude of health needs, a public health crisis is looming. Floodwaters have also shifted explosive remnants of war left over from years of conflict, posing a risk to residents and displaced people.

As at 6 October 2023, there were 2380 cases of acute diarrhoea and 5 cases of bloody diarrhoea reported in the flood affected areas. The epidemiological situation in flood-affected areas has been reportedly stable since December 2023, with no increase in waterborne diseases reported.
trigger:
- The impact of Storm Daniel
- WASH infrastructure damage
- Water contamination
- Overwhelmed health sector
vulnerability: The people affected have been facing the impact of protracted conflict and civil war and are vulnerable to further shocks. Among the affected population are sub-Saharan migrants and asylum seekers, who are considered the most vulnerable.

risk_title: Increased intercommunal conflict and militia attacks in southwestern DRC trigger new displacements and worsen the humanitarian crisis
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Since June 2022, a customary land tax dispute between two communities in Kwamouth territory, Mai-Ndombe province, has gradually escalated to intercommunal violence between the so-called “native” and "non-native" communities. At least 300 people have been killed and more than 161,000 displaced since. In early 2023, the emergence of a communal militia called Mobondo, mainly composed of people from the Yaka and allied communities, marked a change in the conflict dynamics until then marked by sporadic clashes between communities. The Mobondo militia have repeatedly attacked people from rival communities, mainly Teke. Regular clashes between the Mobondo militia and the Forces armées de la république démocratique du Congo (FARDC) have also caused population displacements. Although their number is unknown, the Mobondo militia maintains an active presence in several areas in the west of the country, presumably to gain access to land and natural resources.
Violence by the Mobondo militia, is likely to intensify in the coming months despite FARDC military operations launched since May 2023. The increase of attacks in Mai-Ndombe, Kwilu, Kwango, Kongo-central provinces and Kinshasa periphery in recent months, illustrate the propensity of the militia to strengthen its presence. The periphery of DRC’s capital city Kinshasa is particularly exposed to this surge in violence namely because of the Mobondo militia being already active in the surrounding provinces. 
The recurrent attacks by the Mobondo militias, which the Congolese army do not seem contain, will likely trigger the creation of community self-defence groups as is often the case in the DRC. Many youths in areas already affected but also in the outskirts of Kinshasa will likely join these self-defence groups to protect their own communities. This would lead to an escalation of the conflict, growing insecurity in western DRC and increased violence against civilians. While access and use of land already triggers many conflicts, the involvement of other communities could renew preexisting tensions, further expanding the geographic scope of violence.
trigger: Emergence of ethnic militia, increased attacks against civilians, expansion of the geographical scope of the Yaka-Teke intercommunal conflict
vulnerability:
Dependence on agricultural activities as main livelihood

Non-functional social services due to insecurity

Return of displaced populations to areas that are not yet secure

risk_title: Conflict escalation due to the complete withdrawal of the MINUSMA leads to protection concerns and reduced humanitarian access in northern and central Mali
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The withdrawal of the United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilisation Mission in Mali (MINUSMA) has been decided by the UN Security Council on 30 June 2023, at the request of the Malian transitional government. The departure of the UN mission of around 13,000 forces, is expected to be completed by end of 2023. The departure coincides with growing tensions between the Malian government and an alliance of Tuareg armed groups signatories of the 2015 Algiers peace agreement also known as Cadre stratégique permanent pour la paix, la sécurité et le développement (CSP-PSD). MINUSMA had facilitated interaction between the two parties during the peace talks. The withdrawal of the UN mission could accelerate the end of the ceasefire between the Malian army and the armed groups signatories of the peace agreement, causing a renewal of this conflict in the north of the country .  
The takeover by the Malian army of military bases left by MINUSMA will likely cause an intensification of tensions with the armed groups signatories to the Algiers agreement, which controls large areas of northern Mali. Several security incidents have already been reported during the first phase of the handover. The second phase, which is underway and should lead to the transfer of the bases of Tessalit, Aguelhok and Kidal to the Malian army, could trigger more clashes . MINUSMA’s presence deterred the activity of armed groups in certain areas and guaranteed protection to civilians fleeing attacks in their villages. 
The departure of the mission will also further expose urban areas, where most of the bases are located, to attacks by Islamist armed groups. Armed groups such as the Islamic State in the Greater Sahara and the Jama'at Nusrat al Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM) are likely to exploit the security vacuum left by MINUSMA to expand their area of influence. These groups already control large areas of central and northern Mali. The French Barkhane forces have already withdrawn from the area in 2022 . The security vacuum left by MINUSMA could also stimulate a multiplication of self-defence groups on a community basis. Such groups already exist in Mali and are accused of multiple abuses against other communities for accessing natural resources, or because of alleged support to armed groups.
trigger: MINUSMA withdrawal; increased tensions between armed groups signatories of the Algiers peace agreement and the Malian government; Increased presence of Islamist armed groups across the country
vulnerability: Limited social services, movement restrictions, overcrowding in host community shelters

risk_title: Diplomatic tensions, economic sanctions, and potential regional conflict further deteriorate the humanitarian crisis
rationale:
Following the 26 July military coup, international condemnations multiplied against the National Council for the Safeguarding of the Fatherland (CNSP) now in power. The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) has strongly expressed its disapproval and imposed economic sanctions on Niger. 
ECOWAS has also indicated that it does not rule out resorting to a military solution to restore constitutional order. The “standby force” of the regional organisation has been mobilised for a potential military intervention. A diplomatic solution seems out of reach as Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso have signed a military alliance which provides that any foreign military intervention would be considered an aggression against the other parties and will engage a duty of assistance from all parties .
While several regions of the country are affected by armed groups activity, forcing thousands of people to internally displace or seek refuge in neighbouring countries, a military intervention would escalate in a regional armed conflict. Although it is quite unlikely at this stage, a military intervention would significantly increase the number of people in need of humanitarian assistance while heightening humanitarian access constraints across the country .
trigger: Military coup, ECOWAS sanctions, military alliance between Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger
vulnerability: Thousands of people already displaced living in poor condition, insecurity in conflict -affected areas, several sectoral needs unmet for people affected by conflict and climate hazards

risk_title: Village and youth council elections in Mindanao islands trigger violence among rival groups leading to internal displacements and need for assistance to IDPs
rationale:
Rationale:

Barangay (which is a native Filipino term for a village) is the smallest administrative division in the Philippines. Sangguniang Kabataan is a regional council that represents youth in a barangay. Village and youth council elections are scheduled to be held on 30 October 2023 across the country. 

The village and youth council elections will significantly heighten electoral violence in Mindanao islands, especially in the BARMM region. For the BARMM, these elections are going to be the precursor for the first parliamentary elections to be held in 2025. Nearly 1,000 villages, out of the nearly 2,600 villages, in the region have been classified as potential violence hotspots by law enforcement agencies due to intense political rivalry among local election aspirants, clan politics and feuds, and the presence of non-state armed groups. 
 
Overall, electoral violence in the Philippines is a recurrent concern. 

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) have also been reported to be closely monitoring 300 villages in the Zamboanga Peninsula, the Caraga Region, the BARMM, the Bicol, Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), and Central Luzon regions due to presence of non-state armed actors.

Impact:

The aforementioned elections will trigger electoral violence, among the rival groups participating in the elections, and insecurity in the Mindanao islands. Based on past security incidents, this will lead to civilian casualties and internal displacements, raising protection concerns and the need to provide shelter, food, non-food items, medicines, and health services to the internally displaced population. The government and the humanitarian responders have usually been able to provide assistance to the displaced people in previous violence incidents among rival clans. 

Local officials were targeted in security incident in the past general and mid-term legislative elections. This pattern is expected to hold for the village and youth council elections. 

Update:
The risk has not materialised. No significant humanitarian needs were reported. 
There were pockets of electoral violence during the electoral period of the village and youth elections in the Mindanao islands.  The Commission on Elections reported that 19 people killed and 14 others injured in election violence, mostly in the BARMM. 

Candidates for and winners of the village council elections were targeted during the electoral violence. Very few people have been displaced during the electoral period and post-election violence.  

In one incident, close to a hundred villagers were displaced by gunfight between rival two groups in Maguindanao del Norte. The displaced informed that the hostilities between the groups were related to the village and youth elections, where both groups had favoured candidates.
trigger:
- Electoral period for the village and youth council elections has already started and will take place on 30 October 

- History of electoral violence, clan feuds, and political rivalry in the country

- Rival groups participating in the village and youth council elections

- Presence of non-state armed groups
vulnerability:
- Local officials, voters, and families of rival clans are vulnerable to violence and likely to be displaced

- Political violence tend to be concentrated in the rural areas of the BARMM region, so people, especially voters and local officials, in the region’s rural areas likely to be most affected by the electoral violence

risk_title: Increased security incidents between the military junta and the Arakan Army (AA) lead to renewed conflict, further worsening the humanitarian crisis in Rakhine state
rationale:
Rationale:

A resurgence of tensions between the AA and the Myanmar military junta could potentially break the "informal and humanitarian ceasefire" between the two forces agreed in November 2022. In the second half of 2023, a number of security incidents have been reported in Rakhine state, similar to those that occurred in the months leading to the breakdown of the previous ceasefire in August 2022. These incidents include arrests of civilians with ties (or suspected ties) with the AA by the junta and increased military activities, including drone reconnaissance operations and the AA instructing the residents of a township to dig bomb shelters.

Impact:

Intense fighting may resume if such security incidents continue to occur and would have significant humanitarian consequences, such as internal and cross-border displacements; civilian casualties; increased travel restrictions limiting the movement of people, essential supplies, and aid; and rice harvest disruptions, affecting the livelihood of farmers and heightening food insecurity. The impact of Cyclone Mocha that made landfall on 14 May 2023 aggravates such consequences. 

Rakhine's total population is more than 3.4 million. among them, more than 1.6 million people are in urgent need of assistance as per the assessments conducted by the humanitarian community. Resumption of intense fighting will affect the total population and worsen the situation for the people in need. 

Update:
The risk is materialising. On 13 November 2023, the AA launched attacks on the military junta’s Border Guard Police (BGP) outposts which have, so far, been followed by intense armed conflict between the AA and the military junta forces, breaking the informal ceasefire since November 2022. The AA’s attack is considered to be a part of a greater coordinated attack involving other anti-military armed groups in many states and regions in the country. Since 13 November 2023, up until 5 July 2024, there have been around 2,100 fatalities in Rakhine state due to the conflict. The political dynamics of the Rakhine state conflict has also stoked intercommunal tension and violence against the Rohingya population. Humanitarian access in the state has been severely restricted and disrupted due to various issues, including blocked roads and waterways, and attack against and looting of humanitarian facilities.

Up until 25 June 2024, there are more than 260,000 people have been displaced since the escalation of conflict in November 2023.

A significant portion of the recent armed conflict in Rakhine state has taken place around urban areas, which is a new dynamic compared to previous occasions of armed conflict in the state. Previously, IDPs sought shelter in urban areas as they were perceived to be safer. Many of the IDPs are now seeking shelter in various rural locations with limited access to humanitarian assistance.
trigger:
- Rising tensions between the Arakan Army and the military junta

- Increased control of the Arakan Army over Rakhine state which goes against the military junta’s interests
vulnerability:
Groups of people that are most vulnerable to renewed armed conflict and are likely to have least coping capacity are: 
- People who are already in need of urgent humanitarian assistance

- Stateless Rohingya people

- IDPs in Rakhine state

- People who are already food insecure

- Women, children, and the elderly

- People affected by Cyclone Mocha

risk_title: Coordinated offensives conducted by anti-military resistance forces against the military junta intensify armed conflict throughout the country, worsening the protection, food insecurity, health, and education situation
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Rationale:

A coalition of ethnic armed organisations (EAOs) called the Three Brotherhood Alliance (3BA), comprising the Ta'ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), and the Arakan Army, launched a coordinated offensive, named Operation 1027, against the military junta forces in northern Shan state, close to the Myanmar-China border, on 26 October 2023. Statements by the coalition regarding the offensive point to the intention to safeguard the lives of civilians, assert their right of self-defense, maintain control of their territory, and respond to ongoing artillery attacks and airstrikes from the Myanmar military. They also tagged the military junta government as “oppressive” and stated that they intend to eradicate the "military dictatorship", objective which they state is a shared aspiration of the Myanmar population. The main aim of the operation is to dislodge the military junta forces across the northern part of Shan State.

Many junta military camps/bases have been captured by the EAOs' members of the coalition and the junta have been reported to incur heavy losses. In response, the military has retaliated to the offensive with air strikes and other heavy artillery. As per media reports, at least some areas near or along the China-Myanmar border has been captured by the EAOs, including one of Myanmar's five official border trade crossings with China.

As at 6 November, heavy fighting is going on and have resulted in civilian casualties and displacements in northern Shan. Movement along key routes from Lashio, the capital city of northern Shan, has been severely restricted by the military and the EAOs. Mobile communication services have also been disrupted. Such hindrances have affected the mobility, humanitarian access, and communication with affected communities. Humanitarian organisations, including the UN, INGOs and local humanitarian responders, in northern Shan have existing prepositioned relief supplies and will respond once security and access improves.

The National Unity Government (NUG), the government in exile comprising a group of elected lawmakers and members of parliament ousted in the 2021 Myanmar coup d'état, stated that it was also taking part in Operation 1027. Some of NUG’s armed wings, such as the People’s Defence Forces and Mandalay People's Defense Forces, have reportedly participated or are participating in the offensive. 

Operation 1027 has been reported to spread to Sagaing as well. The Kachin Independence Army (KIA), the Arakan Army (AA), and the Kawlin People’s Defense Force launched an attack on military junta bases in Kawlin township, Sagaing region on 3 November 2023. The Kawlin assault, which, as per media reports, has displaced around 50,000 people, was reportedly a part of simultaneous resistance attacks against the military junta forces launched in eight townships across Sagaing and Magway regions. 

Impact:

The offensive by the coalition will not only intensify armed conflict in the northern Shan state and Sagaing but will also have countrywide consequences. Such a coordinated offensive indicates towards enhanced collaborated offensives by many EAOs and anti-coup resistance forces against the military junta throughout the country in the coming months. It is highly likely that the armed conflict will intensify throughout the country. The Myanmar military forces are expected to intensify artillery shelling and airstrikes, worsening the humanitarian situation in the country, especially worsening the protection, food insecurity, health, and education situation.

Update:

The risk is materialising.

Since the start of Operation 1027 at the end of October 2023, the conflict has increased the number of IDPs in the country by around 1.2 million (up until 24 June 2024). 

In February 2024, Myanmar’s military junta activated the conscription law. More civilians will be recruited into the military and armed resistance groups, as many of the civilians would likely join armed resistance instead of the military junta. Up until June 2024, thousands of civilians have been already recruited into the military. This will result in a broader armed conflict.
trigger:
- The offensive named “Operation 1027” by a coalition of three ethnic armed organisations in northern Shan

- Increased territorial control of and collaboration among anti-military resistance forces

- Growing political instability with no sign of cooperation to de-escalate the conflict between the military junta and anti-military forces
vulnerability:
- Displaced people will be exposed to increased protection risks, such as family separation, psychological distress, gender-based violence, and human trafficking. Women and girls are especially vulnerable to protection risks.

- People fleeing the conflict-affected areas to remote locations, such as jungles, are cut off from any services and beyond the reach of humanitarian responders. 

- Intensified conflict will further increase food production gap, heightening food insecurity and malnutrition. 

- Farmers are likely to lose their livelihoods due to the growing conflict

- The young people in Myanmar are at risk of being forcibly recruited into the military. Under the conscription law, all men aged 18-35 and women 18-27 (men aged 18-45 and women aged 18-35 for people with special expertise, such as doctors and engineers) must serve for up to two years and up to five years in a state of emergency, and evading conscription could result in a prison sentence of three to five years.

risk_title: Continued protests across Panama, following the government's approval to exploit a mining area in a biodiverse jungle, result in access constraints and disruption of services and economic activities for some population groups
rationale:
---------BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE-------
The Panamanian government signed a concession contract (arrangement between a public authority and an economic operator) with the Canadian mining company First Quantum Minerals, which allowed the latter to continue operating an open-pit copper mine in a richly biodiverse jungle. Panama’s National Assembly, the country’s legislative body, and the country’s president fast-tracked the contract and approved it on 20 October 2023. 

Since the contract was approved, Panama has been facing protests across the country. Protestors claim the contract was fast-tracked with little public input and lacks transparency, making allegations of corruption of the lawmakers. The protests are being led by construction workers, educators, indigenous groups, and activists, mainly calling for the revocation of the mining contract. Tens of thousands of people have been reported to be participating in the protests across the country. According to the protesters, there are significant environmental risks of the contract, including for the vital water sources required for water consumption.

As at 10 November 2023, the protests have generally been peaceful; ACLED data shows that around 80% of the protests occurring since 20 October 2023 have been peaceful and 20% violent demonstrations which include incidents of clashes between protestors and security forces, use of tear gas to disperse protestors, arrests, vandalism, and robbery. Significant increase in the deployment of security forces has been observed since the protests began. As at 14 November 2023, two fatalities have been reported: an elderly man was apparently frustrated with the blockage and tried to force the protestors to remove a barrier blocking the Pan American highway and then he allegedly opened fire on the protestors, killing two of them.

On 3 November 2023, the National Assembly signed an indefinite moratorium on new mining concessions into law, which also prohibits renewing existing concessions. However, the new law still allows Minera Panama, the Panamanian subsidiary of First Quantum Minerals, to operate. Hence, the protests are still ongoing. The country’s Supreme Court stated that it will consider two lawsuits filed against the renewed contract with First Quantum.

The protests led to countrywide road blockades that have negatively impacted the economy, transportation, food security, education, healthcare, and WASH, and raised protection concerns.
Due to the insecurity caused by the protests, educational authorities closed all schools across the country. 

There have been reports of attack on healthcare, including assault on healthcare personnel, ambulances, and vehicles transporting patients by people among the protestors. On 27 October 2023, the Panamanian National Operations Center requested interinstitutional support to the Red Cross Society of Panama to provide assistance, especially through healthcare services, to the population affected by the protests and blockades. The IFRC has initiated an operation targeting 3,500 people. In several provinces, supplies required for water purification are running low, leading to the risk of clean water rationing. 

Several areas in the provinces of Bocas del Toro, Chiriqui, Darien, Herrera, and Los Santos have reported fuel shortages and rationing of food supplies by supermarkets and stores. An electricity generation company, whose production depends on fossil fuels, has issued warnings of potential controlled power outages to manage the electricity supply.

Rice is the staple food in Panama. Darien, Herrera, Los Santos, and Chiriqui provinces comprise the primary rice producers. Rice mills are unable to distribute their stored rice during the harvest period due to road closures, resulting in considerable losses. Significant loss in perishable goods, including fruits and vegetables, have also been reported due to the inability to sell and transport perishable products to markets and storage facilities.

In early October of 2023, Panama and Costa Rica announced a plan to provide a bus service to quickly move thousands of migrants crossing the Darien Gap through Panama to the Costa Rican border. On 24 October, it was reported that more than 30 buses from Darien to Costa Rica were stranded in the Chiriqui as they could not move forward towards Costa Rica. On 25 October, another 20 buses were not permitted to pass in San Felix, Chiriqui province; as a result, the migrants on the buses started their journey by foot from San Felix to Paso Canoas, Costa Rica.

-----AGGRAVATING FACTORS--------
Copper is the major export good for Panama. Analysts estimate that revoking the mining contract would cut Panama’s GDP growth from a forecast 6% in 2023 to just 1%. So, repealing the mining contract will have significant negative impact on the economy; however, not repealing it would also likely cause significant negative environmental (and consequently economic) impacts. This situation is aggravated by the current drought, exacerbated by a severe El Nino weather system, which has reduced water levels in the Panama Canal, prompting the Panama Canal Authority to implement additional vessel reductions in an effort to conserve water.

--------EXPECTED IMPACT--------
Continued protests will worsen the abovementioned situation, which could lead to a political and socioeconomic crisis in Panama, and possibly to humanitarian consequences for some more exposed population groups, These consequences could include lack of healthcare support, education, and clean water in some areas of the countries. There would also be raising food insecurity concerns, loss of livelihoods, especially among rice and vegetable farmers, and heightening of protection concerns for those participating in protests that become violent. 

--------UPDATE--------
The risk has only partially materialised. The expected impact was not realised. So far, it has not generated humanitarian needs other than those already mentioned in the background and rationale section. 

Panama's Supreme Court of Justice ruled that Panama’s new mining contract with the Canadian company First Quantum was unconstitutional. Following the ruling, the president of the country said that a process to close the Cobre Panama mine was set to begin. Protests have also began to subside after the ruling.

The protests have already had significant impact on the economy. Retail associations estimated a loss of around US$200 million in the first 30 days of protests. Logistics losses are estimated to be around US$4.6 billion. 

Panama’s economy is heavily based on the ability to facilitate the transit of global merchandise, which has been negatively affected by the protests. The logistics sector has been estimated to account for around 20% of the country’s GDP and employs around 10% of the Panamanian workforce.

The protests also have reportedly reduced Panama’s attractiveness as a foreign investment destination. Large losses in the tourism and hospitality sectors have been reported, with many international tourists cancelling their trips to the country through January 2024. 

Shortages in food, fuel, and medicines have been reported in some cities and the government is importing such supplies from neighbouring Costa Rica to fill the gaps.

The company said that it has initiated international arbitration against Panama. Estimates suggest that Panama might have to pay at least US$20-50 billion (25-65% of the country’s GDP) if it loses the case. 

Livelihoods of the mine's employees and the people whose jobs are indirectly related to the mine are considered to be affected. The mine is reported to employ around 6,600 people (more than 5,500 are Panamanians). In total 40,000 jobs, directly and indirectly, are reportedly linked with the mine. 

It is to be noted that, if Panama loses the international arbitration case, which would be compounded by the negative impacts of the closure of the mine, there will likely be significant socio-economic distress in the country.
trigger: - Protests against a concession contract between the Panamanian government and a mining company
vulnerability:
- Children, the elderly people, people with pre-existing medical conditions, and people with disabilities are likely to be more vulnerable as they often need healthcare support

- Children and elderly people exposed to the protest and violence needing mental health and psychosocial support

- Children facing lack of education due to school closures and needing access to mental health and psychosocial support  

- People impacted by the protests and violence, including those who suffered injuries, property damage, and/or interruptions to their daily lives due to blockades and protests

- Migrants in transit, especially the ones who now have to walk to Costa Rica due to road blockades and demonstrations 

- Rice and vegetable farmers and other people involved in the production, storage, and distribution of rice and vegetables 

- Transportation workers who might face loss in livelihood due to transportation disruptions

- Healthcare workers who face violence during protests while trying to reach patients 

- People facing lack of clean water supply

rationale:
