risk_title: Drought conditions due to the El Nino, high rice prices in the international market, and restrictions imposed by India on their rice exports worsen food insecurity outcomes
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
RATIONALE AND IMPACT
Timor-Leste has around 262,000 people facing high acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) as per IPC projections for May - September 2023. The food insecurity situation will be worsened due to certain environmental and economic factors. 

The entire country of Timor-Leste is showing signs of drought due to the ongoing El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) conditions and is forecasted to strengthen and persist until early 2024. Prolonged dry spells will negatively impact agriculture output in the country. The agriculture sector accounts for around 27% (around 63,000) of total employment. Outside of the labour force, around 162,000 people are subsistence foodstuff producers. Rice, maize, cassava, and sweet potato are the main staple crops in the country. The main growing season of maize is in January and rice is March. Drought conditions will affect the yield of these water-intensive crops. 

The international rice prices surged between July and September 2023, which raised the costs of rice within Timor-Leste and the retail prices of imported rice in the country. The surge in rice prices have made it unaffordable for impoverished families in Timor-Leste. People in the country depend heavily on imports of rice, especially imported Indian rice which comprise around 90% of rice imports by Timor-Leste. The Indian government introduced measures aimed at stabilising domestic food prices which included a ban on exports of non-basmati white rice, 20% export duty on non-basmati parboiled rice, and the imposition of a minimum export price. These measures are aggravating the already worsened rice availability and subsequently consumption situation in Timor-Leste. 

Current stock of rice may only cover just over one month of national rice consumption needs. If the country is unable to secure enough rice and nutritious food as soon as possible, there will be further deterioration of the nutritional and food security status among the poorest and most vulnerable Timorese families. 

AGGRAVATING FACTORS
Oil and gas are the main export products in the fuel and mining products category. In 2022, fuel and mining products contributed to more than 80% of total exports. It also contributes to around 70% of total government revenues. Timor-Leste’s real GDP is estimated to fall by around 17% in 2023, primarily due to reduced oil and gas production.  The real GDP is expected to decline by 6% in 2024. The current and short-term economic situation will reduce livelihood opportunities, aggravating the food insecurity situation in the country. 

BACKGROUND
It is to be noted that, around half of the children under five years of age in Timor-Leste are stunted which is one of the highest rates of stunting in the world, and nearly 40% of children under five years of age are underweight.

The last El Nino event in 2015-16 caused a drought in Timor-Leste and affected 80% of the population, with around 40% of households experiencing food shortages and falling into severe food insecurity. According to an estimate, Timor-Leste could see a rise in food insecurity with 300,000 people facing high food insecurity levels (IPC phase 3 and above) in the current El Nino period. If food insecurity levels get similar to the last El Nino event, then more than 500,000 people could face high food insecurity levels (IPC phase 3 and above).

UPDATE
The risk has materialised.

Around 360,000 people (27% of the population) are estimated to face crisis or above levels of food insecurity (IPC 3 and above) in November 2023—April 2024. It is nearly 100,000 more than the projected figure for May—September 2023. Number of people facing emergency level food security (IPC 4) has more than doubled from 7,000 to around 18,600 in the same period. 

Poverty, El Nino induced drought-like conditions, and high food prices were found to be among the primary drivers of food insecurity. 

Rice and maize are the two main staple foods in the country. Timor-Leste has high dependency on imported rice to meet their demand of rice. Price of imported rice was 30% higher in December 2023 compared to December 2022. Maize prices rose by 66% during the same period, and its production is expected to decrease in 2024 due to the impact of El Nino and fall armyworm infestations.

Due to unfavourable weather conditions including the current El Nino event, shortfall in production of rice in the main rice producing and exporting countries are expected, hence leading to limited global rice availability.

The El Nino is expected to have negative impacts on the national and regional rice and maize production in 2024, leading to limited food availability and increased food prices, and reducing agriculture-related livelihood opportunities and household food reserves. The situation is expected to worsen the food insecurity situation in the post-harvest season, May—September 2024, when food access and availability generally improves. The number of people facing crisis or above levels of food insecurity (IPC 3 and above) is projected to rise to 364,000.
trigger:
- Drought throughout the country due to the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) conditions 
- Rise in international prices of rice
- Restrictions imposed by the Indian government on its rice exports, affecting the imports of rice by Timor-Leste
vulnerability:
Vulnerable groups are:
- Members of impoverished households
- Children, especially who are already stunted and/or underweight 
- Pregnant and lactating mothers as they require nutritious food for their and their children’s health
- People with disabilities (4% of the population)
- Subsistence foodstuff producers and their household members
- Agricultural workers and their household members
- People who provide ancillary services to the agriculture sector
- People employed in the production of oil and gas and who provide ancillary services to the oil and gas industries

risk_title: Thousands of Afghan returnees and the onset of winter season, coupled with a weak health system and ongoing Polio outbreak, heighten the risk of a public health crisis
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The prolonged conflict in Afghanistan, coupled with an economic crisis and a significant shortfall in foreign funds, is contributing to the deterioration of its healthcare system, compromising its capacity to effectively respond to emerging health threats. Adding to this, it is the arrival of the winter season, which brings with it a unique set of health challenges. The cold temperatures are increasing the prevalence of acute respiratory illnesses and placing additional strain on an already fragile healthcare system. 
Inadequate access to heating facilities and a Polio outbreak ongoing since January will likely escalate the health risks for the population, particularly for those who have been already affected by Herat earthquake. 

As the country is grappling with its existing humanitarian crisis, over 428,000 Afghan refugees from Pakistan have also returned to Afghanistan following Pakistan’s recently introduced repatriation plan. Most of these returnees are women and children. The returnees at the border are suffering from limited access to food, WASH, and healthcare services. Given the poor state of the healthcare system, particularly in rural areas, the returnees heading to  provinces with poor services and infrastructure, will likely experience a higher level of needs while putting a strain on the already limited healthcare resources. The arrival of such a large number of returnees also increases the risk of the spread of communicable diseases, such as Polio, as Afghanistan and Pakistan are the only countries where the virus remains endemic.
trigger:
-	Onset of winter
-	High number of arrival of Afghan refugees from Pakistan
vulnerability:
-	29.2 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance, with 17.6 million in need of health assistance.
-	84% of the population lives below the poverty line. The inadequate healthcare infrastructure in rural regions compels residents to travel for treatment, leading them to incur additional expenses and resort to borrowing funds. This financial burden further hampers their ability to access essential healthcare services.
-	The situation disproportionately affects women, who experience heightened challenges with the male guardian (Mahram) requirement, resulting in double transportation costs.
-	Afghan refugees returning from Pakistan leave all their assets and have to depend completely on the deteriorating healthcare system in Afghanistan.

risk_title: The impact of the escalation of fighting between Hezbollah and Israel on the Lebanese agriculture and tourism sectors worsens the country’s socioeconomic crisis
rationale:
Fighting between Hezbollah and Israel has escalated since 8 October 2023 following the start of the most recent war between Hamas and Israel on 7 October. Tensions have increased between Israel and Lebanon over Hezbollah’s support for Hamas and Israel’s bombing of Gaza.

Southern Lebanon, specifically its agriculture and tourism sectors, is facing the biggest impact. Southern Lebanon’s land is agricultural, where many crops and trees are grown. Israel’s white phosphorus bombs are burning and polluting this land, damaging crops and trees and affecting farmers’ livelihoods. Unexploded munitions are also affecting the work of farmers. At the same time, insecurity is leading to the displacement of agricultural workers, who normally harvest olives from October–November, resulting in reduced incomes.

Tourism flourished in early 2023, producing the best revenues since 2019. The Lebanese economy depends heavily on the tourism industry, generating around USD 7 billion in 2022. Since the fighting began, however, tourism has been brought to a near-standstill. Fewer tourists are coming to Lebanon because of insecurity, and hotels are receiving fewer bookings. The Christmas season likely produced less revenue than expected, affecting the livelihoods of many people and the country’s economy.
trigger:
- Escalation of clashes between Hezbollah and Israel
- Increased killing and displacement of civilians 
- Use of white phosphorus bombs
- Unexploded munitions
- Increased insecurity
vulnerability: People in Lebanon already face the impact of a deteriorating economy, high inflation, and livelihood losses. They are generally resilient to human-driven and climate crises, but an increase in clashes and displacement can increase their current needs and vulnerabilities caused or aggravated by the socioeconomic crisis.

risk_title:
DRC general elections trigger heightened levels of violence, leading to 
increasing protection threats, population displacement, and food insecurity
rationale:
The DRC’s Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) has officially set the general elections’ ballot date to 20 December 2023, which will include polls for the presidency, national legislature, provincial assemblies, and local councils. The electoral process started in December 2022 with voter identification and registration procedures that lasted until June 2023. The electoral campaign for the presidency started on 19 November and finish on 18 December, two days before voting day. The electoral process will then continue throughout 2024 with the swearing-in of the new president scheduled for 20 January and indirect elections for the senate, provincial governorates, and other official positions scheduled to take place through September 2024. The presidency, elected through a simple majority for a five-year term, will have President Félix Tshisekedi seeking re-election amid a list of 26 opponents, including prominent figures such as Martin Fayulu, a politician claiming to have won the 2018 elections; Moïse Katumbi, a wealthy businessman and politician; and Denis Mukwege, an activist and 2018 Nobel Peace Prize winner.

Logistical challenges, criticism towards the electoral commission for its alleged biases, and a defective electoral roll generate a climate of mistrust and heightened tensions, compounded by the failure of the Government and the CENI to engage with civil society observer missions. This tense situation engenders an environment that is ripe for discontent, hostility, and protests, increasing the probability of violence during the electoral cycle. The opposition’s reluctance to engage in the electoral process may lead to intentional election disruptions, also potentially instigating violence. At the polling stations, any denial of voter rights, perceived impartiality of officials, or restrictions imposed on observers could lead to confrontations involving officials, supporters of different political parties or rival groups, and security forces.

The tense political environment is heightening social and political divisions. Unresolved grievances from the 2018 contested general elections, which included some of the candidates for the current ballot, have fostered divisions and mistrust among political factions and communities. The opposition is still unsuccessfully discussing the potential for a joint coalition candidate. The fractured opposition landscape, marked by diverse political ideologies and ambitions, has been a source of tension during the electoral process. The fragmentation and lack of meaningful electoral odds for some opposition candidates can lead to frustration among supporters who may feel disenfranchised, increasing tensions and the potential for confrontation 
between rival political factions. Confrontations could also arise if results are contested. A re-elected incumbent and disputed results could trigger existing contentions between communities and ethnic groups to escalate into political violence. A losing party’s refusal to accept the results could incite confrontations and protests involving groups in dispute for prominence and power, potentially escalating into greater clashes between rival communities and largerscale political conflicts. In certain territories, communities are deeply politically attached to particular candidates, such as the Kasaï, who support the incumbent president, and the Katanga, who support Moïse Katumbi, one of the main opposition candidates. These divides could lead to strong reactions. The constant inflammatory language of the Government and opposition figures, including contentious debates around the definition 
of the Congolese identity, amplifies ethnopolitical and intercommunal tensions and divisions and heightens the threat of confrontations.

Continued repression and abuses by state security forces could trigger increased resistance and dissatisfaction, sparking demonstrations, civil unrest, or violent clashes. Reports of military abuse and limits on political freedoms provoke resentment and erode trust in both state institutions and the electoral process. At the same time, heavy-handed security responses and peaceful protest suppression are expected to result in further demonstrations 
and civil unrest.
trigger: 1. Increasing concerns about lack of transparency and fairness in the electoral process; 2. Increasing tensions and societal division; 3. Rising governmental repression and abuses by security forces
vulnerability:
Conflict is a major displacement driver in the DRC. As at the end of October 2023, nearly seven million IDPs lived in the country, a number that has been growing every year. Approximately 81% of these IDPs – about 5.6 million people – lived in the eastern provinces, particularly in Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, and Tanganyika. Nearly five million IDP returnees also lived in 
those same eastern provinces. In October–November 2023, more than 450,000 people fled their homes in Rutshuru and Masisi territories, in North Kivu, because of violence and widespread human rights violations by armed groups. Shelters have been insufficient in responding to the increasing demand. At the same time, authorities have been closing IDP sites in the 
region. Most IDPs are accommodated within host communities, which often struggle to access basic goods and services, creating precarious living situations. Women and girls are at particular risk of gender-based violence (GBV), reports of which have been increasing. Between January–June 2023, nearly 35,000 survivors accessed GBV support services in Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu provinces, but the actual number is probably much higher 
given underreporting, social stigma, and fear of retaliation.

Between July–December 2023, an estimated 25.4 million individuals – 23% of the country’s total population – have been facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity or worse, including 3.5 million people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) levels. The locations with the highest number of people in IPC 3 and above are North Kivu province (2.6 million) and Kinshasa city (2.1 million). The most affected populations are the displaced, host families, returnees, and people whose livelihoods, such as agriculture, have been disrupted by conflict or natural hazards (e.g. flooding). The DRC has some of the highest acute malnutrition rates globally, affecting about 6.4 million people, and one of the world’s highest infant mortality rates. Four women die every hour during labour or from pregnancy-related conditions. Other health challenges, including preventable epidemics (such as measles, yellow fever, cholera, and malaria), aggravate these conditions. Poor infrastructure, health access constraints, and low vaccination coverage contribute to high health needs among the population.

Funding limitations and severe access restrictions because of insecurity and poor basic infrastructure constrain the humanitarian response, making it insufficient to address the affected population’s critical needs. UN agencies estimate that around 200,000 displaced people in the eastern regions are currently cut off from aid because of the major road obstructions resulting from conflict.

risk_title: The impact of war in Gaza and the Red Sea blockade on Egypt’s economy limits access to food and increases malnutrition levels among children
rationale:
Egypt’s economy is suffering from currency floating and record-high inflation rates, which reached 38% in September 2023. The continuing war in the Gaza Strip will likely lead to its further deterioration despite a slight improvement in inflation rates since October.

Tourism revenues have dropped since October because of insecurity at the border area between Gaza and Egypt. Between October–December, ticket purchases for Egypt fell by 26% compared to the same period in 2022. Some rockets from either Israel or Yemen have been misfired and dropped over touristy cities in Egypt, such as Dahab.

The Red Sea blockade also reduces the number of ships passing through the Suez Canal, reducing Egypt’s revenues from transit fees. The canal contributes one-fourth of the country’s currency earnings. Traffic through Bab Al Mandib Strait was estimated to have dropped by 35% as at mid-December. Despite the Houthis claiming to block only ships headed to Israel, some major shipping companies have suspended all of their travel through the Red Sea for security reasons. In case of clashes between the Houthis and the US Navy, a total blockade of the Red Sea will likely take place, largely affecting Egypt’s economy. Generally, shipping and insurance costs have increased, leading to an increase in the commodities also meant to reach Egypt.

An estimated 60% of the population lives near or below the poverty line and is already struggling with the high prices of food items, such as meat and sugar. Prices will likely increase further with the impact of the war in Gaza and the Red Sea blockade, reducing people’s access to food and increasing malnutrition levels. In 2019, malnutrition accounted for 35% of the diseases affecting children below the age of five.

The forced displacement of the Gazan population (about 2.3 million) towards the Sinai Desert in Egypt would further aggravate the crisis and put a strain on Egypt’s public services and economy. The Government will likely need to provide shelter, health, education, and livelihood services to the new refugee population. Some security concerns can arise as well, since new Palestinian factions will likely form (or old factions can reform), leading to clashes on the border with Israeli forces. The impact will further destabilise Egypt and its peace treaty with Israel, affecting the country’s economy.
trigger:
- Further escalation of the war in Gaza
- Movement of Gazan refugees towards Egypt
- Total blockade of the Red Sea
- Increased inflation rates
vulnerability: An estimated 60% of the population lives near or below the poverty line and is already struggling with high food prices.

risk_title: Violence and coercive conditions by Israel in the West Bank result in an uprising, generating Palestinian protection and livelihood concerns
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The intensification of coercive conditions and economic challenges in the West Bank since 7 October 2023, coupled with rising tensions given the military operation in Gaza, risks starting a new uprising in the West Bank. The Palestinian Authority, which could eventually intervene and prevent such an uprising, is losing legitimacy and power, especially with the fiscal challenges that might affect its ability to pay for the security forces in the West Bank.

An uprising would result in the Israeli authorities tightening physical and administrative measures in the West Bank. This would restrict humanitarian activities and access. It would also hamper the implementation of infrastructure development and rehabilitation projects, aggravating an already deteriorated socioeconomic situation.

Military operations, checkpoints, and movements restrictions for people and goods would worsen the economic situation and increase the poverty level in the West Bank. These would also reduce revenue for the Palestinian Authority and its ability to pay for salaries, social assistance, and protection programmes, including the Palestinian National Cash Transfer Program.

Intensified violence in the West Bank would also have a significant impact on protection needs. Protection concerns in the West Bank remain extremely high and are expected to increase given the continued use of excessive force by Israeli forces and Palestinian security forces.

Additionally, Israel can react to any violent uprising with raids targeting Palestinian armed groups. The raids often affect the refugee camps in areas where these groups are active. Increased conflict in and around refugee camps affect the ability of humanitarian organsations to access people in need. In general, Israeli forces often target facilities and assets providing services to Palestinians, such as health facilities and ambulances. Heightened insecurity would limit service provision for groups already experiencing high socioeconomic vulnerabilities.
trigger:
- On 29 December 2022, the Likud and ultranationalist parties led by Benjamin Netanyahu formed a new Israeli Government. Tensions and the escalation of violence in the West Bank have increased since the arrival of this new Government. 

- On 7 October 2023, hostilities erupted in Gaza following Hamas attacks on Israel, triggering intense violence and coercive conditions by Israel in the West Bank, such as movement restrictions between and within towns and cities.

- New armed groups in the West Bank have increased their activities in the West Bank in recent years. Since 7 October 2023, the Israeli raids targeting armed groups in the West Bank have significantly increased, leading to fatalities and infrastructure damage. The Israeli Government has also relaxed its gun laws, making it easier to obtain gun licenses and leading to a noticeable surge in Israeli gun ownership, especially among settlers in the West Bank. This has further increased the potential for violence escalation in the territory.

- Around 152,000 out of the 160,000 Palestinians from the West Bank who worked in Israel or Israeli settlements have not been able to access job opportunities in Israel since 7 October 2023. In 2022, 22.5% of employed Palestinians from the West Bank were employed in Israel and Israeli settlements.
vulnerability:
- The Israeli occupation of the West Bank continues to generate severe humanitarian needs among the Palestinians in the territory. Around 900,000 people in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, are in need of humanitarian assistance. Protracted conflict, the Israeli military occupation, violations of international humanitarian and human rights laws, internal Palestinian political divisions, and periods of escalating hostilities continue to drive humanitarian needs.

- The protracted humanitarian crisis in Palestine has resulted in acute humanitarian consequences – including lack of access to services and displacement. People in need face a lack of adequate health assistance given an overburdened healthcare system, inadequate shelters, food insecurity, and increased poverty and unemployment.

- Palestinians in the West Bank face serious protection challenges, including threats to their lives, liberty, security, property, and freedom of movement, with a lack of accountability and effective remedies.

risk_title: Red Sea shipping disruptions result in the DFA’s designation as Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO), challenging humanitarian operations in northern Yemen
rationale:
Continued Red Sea shipping route disruptions by the DFA and the pressure by several US senators and foreign governments in the Middle East for harsher sanctions on the Houthis increase the likelihood of the US listing the DFA as an FTO. Around 70–80% of the Yemeni population lives in the areas under DFA control, and it will be challenging for humanitarian organisations wishing to operate in the DFA-controlled areas to avoid engaging with the DFA, including for day-to-day transactions.

The US FTO designation of the Houthis is expected to deteriorate the humanitarian crisis in Yemen, as it will lead the private sector and financial institutions to limit their activities in the country. This will increase insurance and operation costs and disrupt supply chains in Yemen, leading to shortages in commodities and increased food prices. Yemen depends on imports to meet 90% of its food needs. The FTO designation would also restrict remittance transfers, which make up 20% of the country’s GDP, from outside Yemen. This will limit Yemenis’ ability to meet their essential needs.
trigger:
In November 2023, the de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) started disrupting the shipping routes in the Red Sea. The DFA claims that the disruption comes as an effort to pressure Israel to stop its military operation in the Gaza Strip that started in October 2023. As at 31 January 2024, the disruptions were still taking place and had forced traffic through the Red Sea to drop by more than 40%.

Since 12 January, the US, along with a coalition of other countries, has responded by striking DFA targets in Yemen. On 17 January, the US declared the Houthis as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT) organisation, which will become effective mid-February. This designation authorises the US Treasury to freeze the organisation's assets and restrict most transactions involving the organisation within the US financial system. Regardless, the DFA has vowed to continue disrupting the shipping routes in the Red Sea and target US interests in the region until the Israeli military operation in Gaza stops.

There is pressure inside and outside the US to designate the Houthis as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO). The push mainly comes from several US senators and foreign governments in the Middle East allied with the US. The FTO designation, unlike the SDGT, would entail sanctions and subject individuals to criminal liability for offering material support to the Houthis. ‘Material support’ is a legal term encompassing the provision of tangible or intangible property or services, excluding medical and religious materials. Examples include monetary instruments, training, lodging, and transportation. At the same time, with the FTO designation, any licences and exemptions issued by the US Treasury under SDGT regulations would not provide protection to organisations and individuals from the consequences of potentially engaging with an FTO entity.
vulnerability: Yemen is already facing a humanitarian crisis, with high food insecurity levels across the country. Around 17 million people, more than half of its population, are facing acute food insecurity and need food assistance in 2023. This figure includes around 2.2 million children and 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women. Over six million of these people are estimated to be facing Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food insecurity levels. Hajjah and Al Jawf in northern Yemen under the DFA and Ta’iz in southwestern Yemen on the front line of the conflict are the most food-insecure governorates in the country.

risk_title: The halt of WFP assistance in Malawi given limited resources increases food insecurity and protection concerns for refugees
rationale:
In January 2024, WFP in Malawi announced that it might stop providing assistance to refugees starting in June given limited resources. This decision could lead to a rise in food insecurity among refugees, particularly in the Dzaleka refugee camp. The Dzaleka refugee camp is overcrowded, with more than 50,600 refugees as at May 2023. The camp was originally established to accommodate up to 12,000 refugees.

In July 2023, WFP reduced food assistance in the form of cash transfers from the equivalent of a 75% ration to a 50% ration. This, combined with the Government's strict encampment policy in May 2023, has made refugees in the camp even more vulnerable to food insecurity. As at November 2023, 78% of the refugee population in Dzaleka needed humanitarian assistance, including for food.

Increased food insecurity could also increase malnutrition levels among the refugees and affect their coping mechanisms, which include leaving the camp to seek other means of livelihood. This could expose them to protection concerns, such as arrest and detention, given the Government's recent enforcement of the encampment policy. Refugee children may be compelled to drop out of school, increasing their risk of child labour and early marriage to support their families.
trigger: WFP halt of humanitarian assistance to refugees
vulnerability:
As at November 2023, 78% of refugees in Dzaleka were food-insecure.
There is a strict encampment policy for refugees.

risk_title: Increasing trend in tribal fighting and availability of modern weapons will heighten protection concerns in the Highlands region of Papua New Guinea
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Rationale:
The elections of 2022 resulted in political and electoral violence between rival political groups and tribal clans in the Highlands region of Papua New Guinea. Such incidents have internally displaced thousands of people. The country lacks the of provision of basic services for its people, and increased tribal fighting would widen such gaps.

In the past, tribal warfare had some rules that were respected by warring parties and did not permit the damage and destruction to public infrastructure, facilities providing basic services such and health and education, and houses, and harming and killing of women and children which has been observed in recent years (especially 2022 and 2023). In the past, the decision to go to war with rival clans or tribes would have been taken collectively. Now, the people, especially young men, tend to go to war against their enemies without maintaining such process.

The past few years have witnessed the use of modern firearms, bombs, and tear gas, instead of bow and arrows, and other traditional weapons used in the past. This has changed the dynamics of the clashes and increased casualties significantly.

The number of armed clashes, riots, and incidents of violence against civilians in the Highlands region in 2023 was significantly higher than in 2021 and 2022. It increased by around 160%, with related fatalities increasing by nearly 230%, compared to 2022. The trend is expected to continue in 2024, which has been the case as at 16 February 2024, until adequate measures by the state to reign in the violence. 

Expected impact:
- Continued tribal fighting would result in heightened protection concerns, including increased violence against women and children and civilian casualties, damage and destruction to houses and public infrastructure, and displacement, including to remote places, such as mountains, with low access to basic necessities. The people affected by the conflict would also require shelter, health, WASH, livelihood, and food and water assistance. 
- Based on past events of violence and related displacements, especially that of 2022, more than 80,000 people could be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2024 and 2025.
trigger:
- Breakdown of rules based tribal warfare
- Increased availability of modern weapons
- Socioeconomic vulnerabilities
- Lack of capacity of security forces
vulnerability:
Vulnerability and coping capacity:
- The country is marked by socioeconomic concerns such as high youth unemployment, reduced purchasing power, limited water, sanitation, and electricity services, very high proportion of children showing stunted growth affecting brain development, poor education system, and high illiteracy rates. Such issues limit people's livelihood opportunities and make them very vulnerable to shocks. 
- Papua New guinea is regarded to be a very dangerous place for women and girls. The number of reports of physical violence against women and girls is significant and is reported to be increasing in the country. Laws designed to protect women and children are rarely enforced due to lack of police capacity. 
- The overall state of the healthcare system is very poor, with lack of trained personnel, inadequate wages, a deteriorating infrastructure, and frequent lack of critical drugs and dressings. 
- It is to be noted that the above issues are more profound in the Highlands region.
- The Highlands region is remote and tend to have severe humanitarian access constraints. The constraints are aggravated during conflict as roads/areas become conflict-ridden and impassable. 

Vulnerable groups:
- Women, especially pregnant and lactating women, single caregivers, the elderly, children, and persons with disabilities
- Internally displaced people

risk_title: Deteriorating socioeconomic situation in Papua New Guinea trigger violent incidents such as riots in urban areas, heightening protection concerns
rationale:
Rationale:
Papua New Guinea is marked by high youth unemployment and poverty, reduced purchasing power, lack of provision of basic services for its people, and poor governance. Only a quarter of the population who are engaged in work have formal, stable jobs. Many people reportedly flee from the violence-affected Highlands region to seek refuge and opportunities in urban centres, especially the capital of Papua New Guinea, Port Moresby. 

Nearly 60% of women and girls aged 15—49 have experienced some form of physical sexual violence, which is almost twice the global average. The overall state of the healthcare system is very poor, with lack of trained personnel, inadequate wages, a deteriorating infrastructure, and frequent lack of critical drugs and dressings.

Such underlying factors are considered to trigger social disruptions. In January 2024, the police went on strike over underpay, which was later revealed to be a technical glitch in the public servants’ payroll system. The initially peaceful protests turned into riots, comprising mass opportunistic looting, arson, and violence, mainly in Port Moresby. At least 15 people were killed in the riots, with some reports indicating a much higher number. Widespread sexual violence was also reported. 

Protests, riots, and incidents of violence against civilians in the non-Highlands areas rose significantly in 2023. The fragile social and economic situation may trigger more violence incidents, particularly riots, in non-Highlands urban centres in 2024. Lack of security forces’ capacity to deal violence also serves as an aggravating factor for riots.

Expected impact:
- The main impact would be heightened protection concerns and healthcare needs, especially for women and children. Women are girls would become increasingly vulnerable to physical and/or sexual violence in periods of violent riots. 
- Access to healthcare services, especially for women and girls, is also very lacking in the country; women and girls would need urgent healthcare assistance in times of riots.
- The violence-affected people would also require food and water, education, WASH, healthcare services, and safe shelter providing protection from violence. Infrastructure for such services are already very poor. Violence would disrupt the existing services and the affected population would urgently require such services.
- As shops in the urban centres are usually targeted during mass looting, their owners and employees are likely to be in need of livelihood support when riots occur.
trigger:
- Continued fragile social and economic situation in the country
- Past events of violent riots in the country
- Possible unpopular government policy or sustained ineffective government policy
vulnerability:
Vulnerability and coping capacity:
- The country is marked by socioeconomic concerns such as high youth unemployment, reduced purchasing power, limited water, sanitation, and electricity services, very high proportion of children showing stunted growth affecting brain development, poor education system, and high illiteracy rates. Such issues limit people's livelihood opportunities and make them very vulnerable to shocks.
- Papua New Guinea is regarded to be a very dangerous place for women and girls. The number of reports of physical violence against women and girls is significant and is reported to be increasing in the country. Laws designed to protect women and children are rarely enforced due to lack of police capacity.
- The overall state of the healthcare system is very poor, with lack of trained personnel, inadequate wages, a deteriorating infrastructure, and frequent lack of critical drugs and dressings.
- Shop owners in urban centres tend to not have enough capital to recover from riots which has been the case for the January 2024 riots.

Vulnerable groups:
- Women, especially pregnant and lactating women, single caregivers, the elderly, children, and persons with disabilities
- Shop owners and shop employees in urban centres, especially Port Moresby, as urban shops are usually targeted by rioters.

risk_title: The escalation of hostilities around Syunik marz between Armenia and Azerbaijan renews wide-scale conflict, resulting in displacement and humanitarian needs
rationale:
Tensions between Armenia and Azerbaijan have been increasing since Azerbaijan swiftly took control of Nagorno-Karabakh region on 16 September 2023. The most recent escalation occurred from 12–13 February 2024, with an attack by Azerbaijan's forces killing four Armenian soldiers. Azerbaijan claimed that the attack was in response to an earlier Armenian attack injuring one of their soldiers.

Azerbaijan's recent increase in demands for Armenia to allow for a land corridor through the Armenian Syunik marz aggravates the tension between the two countries. The corridor would connect the Azari Nakhichevan enclave with Azerbaijan’s mainland; Armenian territories currently separate these two areas. The Azeri population has also asked not to have Armenian custom checks in the land corridor. As a basis for the demand, Azerbaijan has been referencing a provision in the 2020 peace treaty emphasising unimpeded transport connections in the region.

Rhetoric around conflict between the two countries has intensified in the past few months, with Armenia's Prime Minister suggesting that Azerbaijan is preparing to invade Armenia. Armenia has also proposed a mutual arms control mechanism and a non-aggression pact, both dismissed by Azerbaijan as diversionary tactics.

On the international front, Russia has historically been an ally to Armenia in the conflict with Azerbaijan, with Armenia being a member of the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organisation. Russia has previously intervened to ease tensions and deter Azerbaijan from acting on its territorial claims. In the past few years, however, the relationship between Armenia and Russia has been deteriorating, especially after the Russian peacekeeping mission in Nagorno-Karabakh did not effectively break the blockade by the Azeri forces that started on December 2022, which later resulted in the Azeri forces taking over the region in September 2023. This strain is evident in Armenia's decision to freeze its participation in a Russia-led security bloc as part of efforts to distance itself from Moscow in favor of new alliances with European countries, such as France.
trigger:
- Azerbaijan's recent increase in demands for a corridor through the Armenian Syunik marz (region)
- Azerbaijan taking control over Nagorno-Karabakh region on 16 September 2023 in a one-day lightning military operation
- In February 2024, the Azerbaijani attack that killed four Armenian soldiers
- Armenia's Prime Minister suggesting that Azerbaijan is preparing for an invasion
- Azerbaijan dismissing Armenia’s proposal for a mutual arms control mechanism and a non-aggression pact
- Armenia's decision to freeze its participation in a Russia-led security coalition
- New arm deals between Armenia and France
vulnerability: On 16 September, Azerbaijan took control over Nagorno-Karabakh region in a one-day lightning military operation, causing more than 101,000 of the region’s 120,000 people to flee to Armenia as at late 2023. Around 70% of the refugees from the latest hostilities resided in Yerevan city and the surrounding marzes of Armenia. Most resided with pre-existing networks of relatives, while 40% were housed in temporary government-run accommodations. Although the Armenian Government provides some level of shelter and cash assistance, among other services, the refugees still face multiple challenges and need shelter, protection, health, and education services.

risk_title: Conscription policies implemented by the Myanmar military junta and some EAOs heighten protection concerns throughout the country
risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Rationale: 
On 10 February 2024, Myanmar’s military junta announced the activation of the conscription law enforcing mandatory military service for young people. Evading conscription could result in a prison sentence.

Around 14 million civilians are eligible for conscription. The annual recruitment target is estimated to be around 50,000 to 70,000 people. The activation of the law is considered a response to the loss of military junta troops through deaths, injuries, desertions, and defections in the armed conflict against armed resistance groups, comprising anti-coup resistance forces and ethnic armed organisations (EAOs). 

Similar conscription has also been observed among some of the EAOs, both against and allied with the military, in the northern Shan state, indicating a possible expansion of the warscape in the state. 

It has been widely reported that young people are reluctant to serve in the military under the military junta and some may even join the armed resistance groups instead of the military as, in general, they oppose the military junta. Many other are reported to be reluctant to join any groups that are implementing conscription laws.

There have been reports of people being kidnapped, arrested, or compelled into joining the military and used as human shields in 2023 and 2024. Rohingyas living in the IDP camps of Rakhine state are reportedly a target of the military junta for forced recruitment. There have been reports of people trying to leave the country, especially to Thailand, which has increased the risk of increased refugee influx in Thailand.

Conscription laws implemented by the military junta and some EAOs will likely geographically expand and intensify armed conflict in the country in 2024.

Expected impact:
- Intense armed conflict means heightened protection risks and widespread human rights violations. Civilians would likely face more forced recruitment through arrests and kidnappings, and through various means of coercion. Conflict would also cause more people to be displaced. the country already has around 3 million IDPs, among which 2.7 million were displaced after the military coup in 2021.
- Conscription laws would increase forced migration, especially to Thailand, Bangladesh, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Forced migration would also severely heighten the risk of human trafficking, leading to forced labour and sexual exploitation.
- Recruitment of people serving in the education and healthcare sectors would also have a negative impact on the already poor education and healthcare systems in the country.
- Local humanitarian workers who are staff of NGOs and other humanitarian organisations (especially the ones not registered with the military junta) are also in the ambit of the conscriptions. Recruitment of such people would constrict humanitarian assistance.
- Shift of resources away from productive sectors, decreasing the economic capacity of the country.
- The increase in conflict will likely result in internal displacements.
trigger:
- Number of military junta bases and towns captured by armed resistance groups
- Increase in attacks of the military junta on captured bases and towns captured by armed resistance groups.
- Desertions, defections, surrenders, and fatalities among the military junta soldiers
- Economic, political, and military support provided to the military junta by foreign countries
vulnerability:
Vulnerable groups:
- Young people who are eligible under the conscription (and their families) of the military junta and some EAOs
- Civil servants as they have been reportedly targeted by the military junta for conscription

Vulnerabilities:
- Vulnerability among the country’s population is very high. Some of the major ones are cited below:
- 18.6 million people in need in 2024. The rest of the around 37 million people are affected but not in need. It is very likely that the conscription law will shift people from affected (but not in need) group to people in need group.
- High levels of poverty (nearly 50% of the population living below the national poverty line of 1,590 Kyats a day).
- 12.2 million people already need protection assistance in 2024. 
- The main protection concerns which are also among the main drivers of the humanitarian crisis, e.g., protracted conflict, human rights violations, intercommunal tensions, widespread fear, and institutionalised discrimination, are likely to be aggravated by the conscription law.

risk_title: Post electoral violence in Tunisia results in civil unrest, economic disruption, and population displacement
rationale:
Tunisia has been facing an increasingly unstable political environment since at least 2021, following President Kais Saied power grab when he suspended the parliament, granting himself increased political powers. This shift in power as been widely criticised by the Tunisian and has been triggering many protests, especially in light of Tunisia's ongoing economic crisis, including soaring inflation, rising unemployment, and shortages of essential goods due to inability to finance import and consequent lack of foreign currency. The economic crisis was exacerbated by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the economy. 

Presidential elections are scheduled for 6 October 2024. Since August, the Saied administration has engaged in a campaign of repression against political opponents, civil society actors, and media. Many candidates have been disqualified under increasingly strict electoral laws, constraining political competition. The Independent High Authority for Elections (ISIE) has ignored court rulings that would have allowed these candidates to run, leading to accusations of illegitimacy and manipulation of the electoral process. This indicates that Tunisian people and opposition parties and figures will likely not be convinced with the outcome of the elections, especially if it Saied wins. In that case, the results of the election should be contested, but on 27 September, the Tunisian parliament voted in favour of stripping the administrative court authority from its rule in election appeals. This means that contesting the elections result will not possible, already sparking protests in Tunisia. It is also likely that there is going to be a widespread abstention from the elections, reflecting the lack of faith in the electoral process.

As of 7 October, the official election results are not announced yet, but estimates indicate that Saied is likely to win with 89% of votes. There has been no reports of protests yet.

Impact: In the event of Saied announced the winner of the elections, it is likely that it could trigger mass protests and unrest in urban centres like Tunis city, amid fear of going back to levels of tensions, uncertainty, and protests that Tunisia experienced in 2011 during the Arab Spring uprising. Civil unrest may lead to clashes between Saied's supporters and opposition groups, further exacerbating tensions within communities and resulting in injuries and fatalities. The current government is likely to respond with arrests and crackdowns, which could escalate tensions. Violence and insecurity are likely to result in internal displacement and the increase of humanitarian needs such as shelter, food, water, and healthcare. Protests and unrest may also disrupt economic activity, worsening the humanitarian situation by exacerbating shortages of basic goods and services, already an issue in Tunisia due to the shortages in foreign currency.
trigger:
- Inability to contest election results: The exclusion of credible opposition candidates and manipulation of legal mechanisms in a way to support President Kais Saied has heightened public distrust in the election's integrity. It is likely that many Tunisians and opposition leaders will want to contest the election results if Saied wins. However, the inability to do so because of Government regulation issued in September to prevent that will likely fuel protests and civil unrest. 

- Pre-electoral repressive practices: Ongoing repression of political opposition and civil society, including arrests of potential candidates, fuels an atmosphere of tension that is likely to erupt into violence following the elections.
vulnerability: Many Tunisians, particularly those in peri-urban and rural areas, are already struggling with poverty, reduced access to healthcare, and limited public services. This is mainly due to Tunisia’s worsening economy that was exacerbated by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and domestic mismanagement, which all resulted in shortages in foreign currency and increased the government’s inability to import basic goods. Inflation, rising unemployment, and basic commodity shortages—such as food and fuel—are critical issues affecting the population, especially those living below the poverty line. This economic situation leaves people highly vulnerable to the impacts of any political unrest, including violence, strikes, or disruptions in essential services.
